target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers for many voters, especially low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove scheduling barriers because private employers are generally not required to give paid time off, so retail, restaurant, caregiving, delivery, and other service workers may still have to work or lose pay/hours in order to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would be a dependable access reform and a stronger way to improve voting access than other measures.
objection: A holiday is not the most reliable solution; state laws requiring employers to provide time off for voting and administrative reforms like automatic voter registration would more directly address the bottlenecks that prevent people from voting.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would shift the real-world schedule enough to matter even without guaranteed paid leave.
objection: Without an employer mandate, private workplaces can continue operating normally on Election Day, especially in low-income sectors, so the holiday does not reliably create broader, less conflict-prone voting hours.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would meaningfully change employers' and workers' incentives so voting becomes easier during daytime hours.
objection: A calendar signal alone does not reliably change whether private employers schedule people to work; many low-income workers would still face the same work-vs.-vote conflict, so the supposed incentive shift is too weak to solve the barrier.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status would create a common daytime opportunity for voting.
objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to close or give paid time off, so many shift-based workplaces would still operate and low-income workers would still have to choose between voting and working.

target: AG1's claim that broad international practice and public support show a national holiday is an effective way to increase access and turnout.
objection: Public support only shows acceptability, not effectiveness, and OECD comparisons do not prove that a U.S. federal holiday alone would meaningfully improve turnout or scheduling access because other countries differ in many other relevant voting conditions.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday would alter the shared local schedule enough to give workers a usable daytime voting window.
objection: The assumption is weak because private employers in sectors like retail, restaurants, caregiving, and delivery are not required to close or provide paid time off, so the calendar label may change without changing the actual time constraint on workers.
